title: Molecular Orbitals, Bond Order and Magnetism

pages.title: Why is oxygen attracted to a magnet?

blocks.text: A simple Lewis picture pairs all electrons in O₂, yet oxygen is paramagnetic: it is attracted by a magnetic field. Molecular orbital occupation explains the unpaired electrons behind this observation.
We will fill allowed molecular states, count bonding and antibonding electrons, then predict both bond order and magnetic behaviour. Counting alone is not enough; orbital energy order matters.

pages.transition: Identify the molecular states before placing any electrons.

pages.title: Distinguish sigma and pi molecular orbitals

blocks.text: Sigma molecular orbitals have cylindrical symmetry about the internuclear axis. Pi orbitals arise from parallel sideways overlap and occur as two equal-energy orientations for the relevant p orbitals.
Antibonding partners carry a star and contain a node between nuclei. Wave-function signs denote phase, not charge. Two π orientations must obey Hund’s rule when singly occupied.

An MO box still accepts at most two opposite-spin electrons. A pair of degenerateπ boxes is filled singly before pairing. The familiar atomic occupation rules apply, but the boxes now represent states spread over a molecule.

pages.transition: Choose the appropriate ordering for the particular second-period molecule.

pages.title: Use the correct second-period energy order

blocks.text: For Li₂ through N₂ in the elementary ordering, bonding π2p orbitals lie below bonding σ2p. For O₂ and F₂, bonding σ2p lies below bonding π2p.

In both cases, after the bonding 2p set come π*2p and then σ*2p. Choose the correct ordering before filling. A reversed σ/π order can give an incorrect electron arrangement even when the total count is right.

pages.transition: Apply electron-count and spin rules consistently.

pages.title: Fill molecular orbitals using familiar rules

blocks.text: Electrons occupy lower-energy states first, at most two opposite-spin electrons per orbital. In degenerate orbitals, they occupy singly with parallel spins before pairing. These are Aufbau, Pauli and Hund applied to molecular orbitals.
The molecule’s electron total comes from both atoms and any ionic charge. Core bonding and antibonding contributions often cancel in bond-order calculations, but their electrons still exist.

pages.transition: Occupation now gives a quantitative net-bonding measure.

pages.title: Define bond order from occupation

blocks.text: Bond order=(N_b−N_a)/2, where N_b and N_a count electrons in bonding and antibonding orbitals. The half reflects that a pair of bonding electrons contributes one bond.

A positive value indicates net bonding in this elementary model. Greater bond order generally corresponds to stronger, shorter bonds in a related series. A zero value predicts no stable conventional bond in the model.

pages.transition: Test the calculation on the simplest diatomic examples.

pages.title: Compare H₂, He₂ and Li₂

blocks.text: H₂ has 2 bonding and 0 antibonding electrons, so bond order=(2−0)/2=1. He₂ has 2 bonding and 2 antibonding electrons, giving 0, so no stable ordinary He–He bond is predicted.
Li₂ has 6 total electrons: (σ1s)²(σ*1s)²(σ2s)². Bond order=(4−2)/2=1, with all electrons paired. The core 1s contributions cancel but must be counted correctly.

pages.transition: A filled bonding2p set explains nitrogen’s strong bond.

pages.title: Explain nitrogen’s strong bond

blocks.text: N₂ has fourteen electrons. After the core and 2s bonding/antibonding pairs, its six remaining valence electrons fill the two bondingπ2p orbitals and bondingσ2p orbital completely.
Bonding and antibonding totals give bond order 3. All electrons are paired, so N₂ is diamagnetic. The high bond order explains the short, strong N–N bond in comparison with lower-order related bonds.

pages.transition: Oxygen requires a different occupation that explains its magnetism.

pages.title: Explain oxygen’s magnetism

blocks.text: O₂ has sixteen electrons. Its last two electrons occupy the two degenerateπ*2p orbitals singly with parallel spins. It therefore contains two unpaired electrons and is paramagnetic.
Bond order is 2: ten bonding minus six antibonding electrons, divided by 2. The unpaired electrons are in antibonding orbitals; they do not prevent net bonding.

pages.transition: Changing the charge tests the role of antibonding occupation.

pages.title: Predict oxygen-ion comparisons

blocks.text: Removing one electron from O₂ removes it fromπ*2p, increasing bond order from 2 to 2.5 in O₂⁺. Adding one gives O₂⁻ bond order 1.5; adding two gives O₂²⁻ bond order 1.
O₂⁺ and O₂⁻ each retain one unpaired electron; O₂²⁻ has pairedπ* electrons. The related bond-length trend is shortest for O₂⁺ and longest for peroxide O₂²⁻.

Compare O₂⁻ with O₂²⁻. The second added electron completes pairing in theπ* set and lowers bond order from 1.5 to 1. Thus magnetic behaviour and bond strength change for different reasons: pairing controls magnetism, while antibonding count controls the bond-order change.

pages.transition: Check bond order and unpaired-electron count as distinct conclusions.

blocks.text: Bond order comes from bonding minus antibonding occupation. Paramagnetism comes from unpaired electrons; diamagnetism means all are paired. These are related calculations but not interchangeable tests.

Use the correct energy order, conserve the electron total and apply Hund’s rule. Oxygen’s magnetic behaviour is compelling evidence that a molecule-wide orbital description adds information beyond a simple Lewis drawing.

questions.question: Why does O₂ have two unpaired electrons?
questions.answer: Its last two electrons singly occupy the degenerateπ*2p orbitals according to Hund’s rule.

questions.question: Which lies lower for O₂: bondingσ2p orπ2p?
questions.answer: Bondingσ2p lies lower; for lighter Li₂–N₂ the ordering is reversed.

questions.question: Find bond order for 8 bonding and 4 antibonding electrons.
Why does He₂ have bond order zero in this model?
questions.answer: Its two bonding electrons are cancelled by two antibonding electrons.

questions.question: Why does O₂⁺ have higher bond order than O₂?
questions.answer: Ionisation removes an antibonding electron, increasing(N_b−N_a)/2 by 0.5.

questions.question: Which is longer-bonded: O₂ or O₂²⁻?
questions.answer: O₂²⁻, because its lower bond order 1 gives a weaker, longer bond in this related series.

questions.question: Can a positive-bond-order molecule be paramagnetic?
questions.answer: Yes. O₂ is bonded with bond order 2 and also has unpaired electrons.
